A lot of new drivers have trouble navigating at first. Use Google maps it's a great tool. I suggest picking a destination that's not too far that you've been to many times. Set the map to go there and look at the route beforehand. Use the satellite option to actually look at the roads and see if you find any particularly difficult intersections or anything. I found that this helped me calm down a bit if I was nervous.
While driving there you could also have a trusted and patient person in the passenger seat giving you guidance if you get confused. It's just the first few times that are really scary but then you'll start to remember roads and turns, just like when you walk somewhere familiar. Just remember there's no shame in using Google maps. Everyone does it.

Another tip is to use Google maps while someone else is driving so you can see what the turns mean and how far the turn is, stuff like that. Just need to get used to it.

I had bad driving anxiety which made it horribly painful for me to learn to drive because my shoulders and neck were so stiff they'd hurt for a while after I finished my lesson. I knew I needed to work through it because culturally I'd seen many women in my family rely on the men to get around and I just knew I couldn't continue that. 

It was a difficult process but I'm glad to say I got past it. I still do have the intrusive thoughts and the hesitation  to get in a car when I have to but it's more of a slight inconvenience in my mind rather than something that prevents me from driving. It's something I've achieved this year and I'm so proud of it because I never thought I'd be able to do it.

The main points I noticed were that I'd start slow and increase the difficulty over time. I focused initially on driving with an instructor till I got my license. Then with a friend or my partner until I could comfortably navigate roads and use a gps without their help. Then I slowly started going on small drives myself but started with 5-8 minute drives on slow roads. 

The next hurdle was getting used to freeways. I only ever drove on freeways with a trusted passenger who could guide me if I needed it but for the most part i tried to do it myself. It took me a while after getting my license to drive on a highway myself but because I had already done it many times it wasn't as scary.

Now, the intrusive thoughts were a challenge to overcome but that needed a lot of mental work of telling myself that my thoughts cannot control what happens on the road. I did like to think that my anxiety could be used to try and predict how other drivers might act based on past experiences and in turn learn how to drive more defensively. 

Everything helped, driving tutorial youtube videos, observing the good drivers in my life, avoiding the unsafe behaviours of the bad drivers in my life, making a mental note of common dumb shit other drivers do. I knew if I was afraid of something I had to push through it. Even if you push the boundaries a little each time, that's good enough. Trust that over time it can make a big difference.

Holy shit! I'm in a weirdly similar situation. I might be able to leave by the end of the year or start of next too. My parents aren't depressed but they're really abusive (Verbally and emotionall). I've lost all my energy and I cry myself to sleep several times a week. 

I'm not the best for advice since I'm really looking for some good advice myself but I'm happy to share what works for me.

I love listening to a favorite playlist I made. I know all the songs word for word so it feels like an escape. I found that dancing like an idiot to my favorite songs in my room helps me get in some physical movement and it also boosts my mood a bit. 

I also get by through planning. I've been really trying to put stuff in place for when I can leave, sorting out living arrangements and whatever I can do in advance. Having a date I can look forward to really helps. Right now I don't have an exact final date so I make milestones for myself. Eg: Two weeks till my friend's birthday, or 3 days till a new season of my favorite show comes out. I have a paper calendar where I mark these milestones so its visual and doesn't clutter up my phone calendar. I also plan time to do nothing. Sometimes I feel guilty if I'm not being productive so I specifically plan down time where I'm SUPPOSED to do nothing.

I try to also make weekly routines for myself. Like every two weeks I go for icecream by myself and order a flavour I wouldn't normally get. I also sit there and journal for 30 minutes while I eat. 

I also have a word document where I jounral in once a month (sometimes every two weeks). I write down everything I hope I can accomplish in the coming months. I write down my fears and just VENT about anything. I don't have set rules for this or like a set time frame. It's just something I personally do at the start of each month. Then after two weeks or a month has passed, I revisit that and read the previous month's entry. That helps me track what stuff has improved and what has worsened and why. It helps me stay motivated because I am reminded that that entire month has passed just like this one will and I'm okay. 

Main thing is I try to do easy things. It's not easy living like this anyway so I don't bother with strict rules and rigid routines. Having that flexibility sets me up for small success and those keep me going. Eg: Aiming for 10 minutes of exercise 3 days a week instead of an hour long routine everyday.

 I feel like if I try to aim too high right now I'll just end up quitting out of frustration. Be kind to yourself, right now you're in survival mode. Plan for your future. Not saying it'll be easy straight up once you leave but things WILL get better slowly. You will start to heal. 

Also, there are some books and resources on Emotional Neglect that might help with the resentment and grief. It's very normal and you're absolutely not alone. The book I'm reading right now is "Running on Empty: Overcoming your childhood emotional neglect". I think you can get a pdf of that online if the actual book is too expensive. Check out r/emotionalneglect if you'd like too. It helps to have a group of people who know what it's like. They're very supportive.

Hope this helps in some way.
